newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Rift grows between Israel's PM, finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Rift grows between Israel's PM, finance minister.

text.p: The rift created between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Dan Meridor over capital market reform has cast doubts on the government's ability to pass economic measures, analysts said.

"If this is how the government makes decisions it is a major blow to its already damaged prestige and calls into doubt its ability to push through important economic measures, notably the 1997 budget," Pinchas Landau, senior columnist in the Globes economic daily told Reuters. "Meridor ought to resign."
The government envisages a 4.9 billion shekel ($1.54 billion) cut, equal to 3.2 percent of originally planned spending, in the 1997 budget to be submitted to parliament at the end of the month.
The provisional budget for 1996 is 172.8 billion shekels.
The proposal has aroused widespread opposition as critics say the cuts, including the raising of public transport prices and a reduction in child allowances, will hit low-income families hardest.

In the early hours of Monday morning Israel's cabinet adopted only in part the finance ministry's proposal for capital market reform, postponing a decision on a politically-sensitive tax on savings of less than 10 years' maturity, which was a key component of the reform.

The capital market reforms are aimed at diverting short-term savings into long-term alternatives and to stimulate capital markets. Opponents of the tax say it is unwise to tax savings when national savings are falling.
After hours of debate and of strong differences of opinion between Netanyahu and Meridor, a compromise was reached whereby a decision on all measures related to savings would be delayed by two weeks.

Finance Ministry sources said Meridor opposed this decision and called for the immediate adoption of all the recommendations. But a ministry spokeswoman denied media reports that Meridor had threatened to resign.
Members of the committee that recommended the measures have said the entire package of proposals must be implemented if the government is to revive the slumping stock and bond market.
Netanyahu, who took office in June with a promise not to raise taxes, led the cabinet majority in favour of the compromise.
The tax on short- and medium-term savings has been openly opposed by both Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel and the prime minister's office director-general Avigdor Liberman.
Landau said the capital markets will react very negatively to the friction created between Meridor and Netanyahu.

Traders do not expect the market to react significantly to the decision to postpone the vote. "I think the stock market will be indifferent to the compromise," said Gidi Halpern of Meitav Investments and Securities.
"The stock market is completely dead. The decision and the tension between Meridor and Netanyahu will prolong the negative atmosphere," he said.

Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Capital Holdings consultants, said the fact that the cabinet had approved most of the proposals was positive for the market. He also said he believed Netanyahu and Meridor would eventually reach a compromise on savings.

"Although Netanyahu comes out looking very bad, investors' confidence is more dependent on the political situation. If he (Netanyahu) can wrap up the Hebron (redeployment) issue in a week or two it will do much more to return confidence," he said.
Israel's stock market has been severely affected by the stalling of the Middle East peace process and by the recent bloody clashes between Israelis and Palestinians.
($1 = 3.19 shekels).
